newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia premier asks Duma's backing for budget cuts.
newsitem.headline: Russia premier asks Duma's backing for budget cuts.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, facing a serious government shortfall in tax revenues, urged parliament on Wednesday to back plans to slash spending across the board.

Chernomyrdin, reviewing the Russian economy in the first four months of this year, said there were signs of growth in several sectors. Budget revenues had improved in March and April, but spending was still too high.

"The situation in March and April has improved somewhat, but this is still not conclusive," Chernomyrdin told the State Duma, the lower house of parliament. "We have no reason to hope that the situation will improve by itself."
Dismal tax collection and poor budget discipline have created a web of non-payments in the economy. Wage arrears stretching back many months have left millions of people in poverty.

Under a budget law passed last year, the Duma must approve revised spending levels if revenue is more than 10 percent below plan. Chernomyrdin said the government received just 65 percent of its expected income in the first four months of the year.
Expenditure during that time was curtailed to 70 percent of the level planned.

In a clear sign of high tension in relations between the Duma and Yeltsin, Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov who controls the biggest single faction in the chamber urged the Russian leader to replace his reformist government.

"The government is made up of people personally responsible for policies hostile to the population -- impoverishment and rip-off privatisation. We must suggest that the president reviews the cabinet," Zyuganov told deputies.
Virtually every deputy spoke out against plans to cut 1997 spending, and many called for new revenues to be raised through ideas such as a national lottery.

But the vote on cutting spending was put off until Friday. One proposal on the agenda would entitle the government to cut spending, so the Duma would not have to take responsibility for the politically unpopular move.
"The government itself should face responsibility for its inability to fulfil the budget," Roman Popkovich, deputy head of the pro-government Our Home is Russia party, told Reuters.
Yabloko head Grigory Yavlinsky was seeking more dramatic action, and told the Duma he had collected 93 signatures calling for a vote of no-confidence in the government.
Yabloko deputies said their motion was aimed at replacing Chernomyrdin with a more active reformer such as Chubais or First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov.

Under Duma rules, such a vote must be put on the agenda within seven days if more than 90 deputies call for it but most deputies, including the communists, have indicated they do not want to topple the government.

Some communist deputies want to double the money supply to provide companies and the government with the cash to pay overdue bills, but Chernomyrdin said the government would never agree to this inflationary move.
